what_it_does: Large cloud providers use machine learning models to automatically balance how much compute resource (CPU time, memory) each server is given; the problem is that these models are trained on historical workload patterns, and when real-world usage shifts to something new (called out-of-distribution data — patterns the model has never seen), the model makes confident but wrong predictions without any warning. The paper studies this failure mode using real production data from Google's fleet, showing specific cases where ML-driven resource allocation goes silently wrong. It evaluates several techniques for detecting when a model is operating outside its training experience — methods based on how far the new data is from the training data, how confident the model's own output scores are, and ensemble approaches (using multiple models and checking if they agree). The paper finds that Bayesian models, which are designed to express uncertainty in their predictions rather than always giving a single confident answer, are particularly effective at flagging cases where a human or a simpler fallback policy should take over.
